Bottom line — brief 13, 2026-09-06
The war restarted. After about a month without a direct exchange the US struck Iran on 1 September, citing a failed Iranian attempt to mine the strait and hit a US base in Jordan, and Iran retaliated across five countries hosting US facilities — Kuwait, Bahrain, the UAE, Jordan and Iraq. The Qatari mediation channel that opened Brief 012's window is dead; Vance says there will be no talks until Iran stops attacking commercial shipping. Iran alleges a US strike killed civilians at a wedding in Sirik: the figures differ between outlets, Vance is 'extremely skeptical', CENTCOM says it does not target civilians, and the claim runs here unresolved. Separately, the one number everyone uses to judge whether Hormuz works is now itself in dispute — Treasury, Energy and the White House cite 10 to 18 million barrels a day while Lloyd's List Intelligence counts about 14 non-Iranian-linked ships a day and JMIC's 1 September advisory calls traffic far below baseline. Brent closed the week near $96, its strongest since mid-July. On Russia, the first reciprocal restraint of the war: Putin ordered a 72-hour pause on Kyiv, Zelenskyy reciprocated on Moscow, and Witkoff and Kushner met Putin for over three hours on 5 September and Zelenskyy on 6 September, with no breakthrough announced by any party. IR moves to 10 and escalating; EU to 6 after Germany formally blamed Russia for the Leipzig airport drone attack.

IRIran / Hormuz10/10 · escalating ▲

The mediation track is gone and the exchange is back, now reaching five countries that host US facilities. Moved to 10 and escalating.

The war restarted. The US struck Iran on 1 September for the first time in about a month, citing a failed Iranian attempt to mine the strait and hit a US base in Jordan; CENTCOM's target set was air defence, radar, maritime assets, mine-laying capability and communications. Iran retaliated on 1-3 September against US facilities in Kuwait, Bahrain, the UAE, Jordan and Iraq. The US struck Iranian oil tankers on 5 September after Navy ships were targeted. Iran alleges a US strike killed civilians at a wedding in Sirik; Vance is 'extremely skeptical' and CENTCOM says it does not target civilians, and the figures differ between outlets — the claim runs unresolved. The Qatari mediation channel that opened Brief 012's window is dead: Vance says there will be no talks unless Iran stops attacking commercial shipping.

RURussia / Ukraine8/10 · volatile ◆

A denied-then-confirmed CIA channel into Moscow, an ICBM test three days later, and another irreplaceable bomber lost at Engels -- movement on every axis except the front line. Held at 8, volatile.

The window's substance was diplomatic and strategic rather than territorial. CIA Director Ratcliffe made an unannounced 25 Aug Moscow visit -- denied by Peskov the same day, later confirmed by the Kremlin, which said Putin was briefed. NYT reporting says he told FSB chief Bortnikov Russia's position worsens without serious talks. Russia test-launched a mobile ICBM on 28 Aug. Ukraine destroyed a second Tu-95MS at Engels-2 in six weeks and Zelenskyy set a 1,000-drone-a-day goal. ISW assesses Russian budgetary strain is producing concrete operational problems and that the MoD is expanding access to personal and medical data ahead of anticipated involuntary reserve mobilisation after the 20 Sept Duma elections. | 6 Sept: a real negotiating round and the first reciprocal restraint of the war, against no announced framework and Zelenskyy saying he expects the war to continue. Held at 8/volatile — large movement in both directions at once, which is what volatile is reserved for.

CNChina / Taiwan6/10 · escalating ▲

The Japan front is now the sharper edge — Tokyo is fielding strike weapons that reach the mainland while Beijing runs sustained coercion.

Structural deterioration with Japan; steady PLA pressure on Taiwan; no invasion assessed as planned. | 29 Aug: no dated China/Taiwan/Japan event was found in the 25-29 Aug window; Taiwan MND's PLA activity page could not be fetched (robots.txt). Held unchanged and the gap is stated rather than filled. | 6 Sept: the PRC foreign ministry invoked the UN Charter 'enemy state' clause against Japan on 2 September and drone activity over the Senkakus and Ryukyus intensified. Rhetorical and gray-zone, not a change in force posture. Held.

KPNorth Korea6/10 · volatile ◆

Quiet window. The 6/volatile reading dates from Brief 011's 19-20 Aug summit-overture-plus-missile-barrage sequence and is only now correctly reflected in the live thread object.

Unchanged this window -- no new DPRK launch or summit development was found between 25 and 29 Aug. Intensity and direction are corrected here to 6/volatile, the values Brief 011 reasoned to and recorded in its archive snapshot but never wrote into threads[]; the live thread object had remained at 5/holding. | 6 Sept: nothing verified moved in this window. The most recent confirmed activity remains the 20 August launch during the US-ROK drills. Held.

HLHomeland / Hemisphere5/10 · escalating ▲

Haiti's 23 Aug Kenscoff attack is worse than first logged -- 47 dead, 52 taken, hostages under an execution threat, and an emergency Security Council session. Held at 5 escalating: a corrected toll on a counted event is not a second escalation.

The 23 Aug Kenscoff attack is now established at 47 killed, 22 injured and more than 52 abducted, per the UN Integrated Office in Haiti -- corrected upward from the '~30 on 24 Aug' Brief 011 carried. More than 50 hostages remain held under an explicit execution threat from the gang leader, and the UN Security Council called an emergency meeting for 28 Aug. Intensity is held at 5, not raised: the revised toll sharpens an event this ledger already counted rather than adding a new one. 5/escalating are also the values Brief 011 reasoned to but never wrote into threads[], which had remained at 4/easing. | 6 Sept: the Gang Suppression Force mandate expires 30 September and Haiti has asked for renewal; nothing has yet been decided. Held pending the Council vote.

TRTerrorism8/10 · escalating ▲

The escalation is broadening rather than deepening — Yemen, the Red Sea and southern Lebanon all moved this week, but no single front crossed a new threshold of intensity.

The UN's own envoy says Yemen is closer to full-scale war than at any point since 2022; the Lebanon front reopened on 15 Aug with the deadliest day since the June truce. | 29 Aug: the 24 Aug Houthi missile strike on the Saudi tanker Amzan off Yanbu is late-filed this brief; no dated Yemen or Lebanon event was found between 25 and 29 Aug. Held unchanged. | 6 Sept: nothing verified moved in this window against this thread's own watch items. Held.

EUEurope / NATO6/10 · escalating ▲

A NATO member has now publicly attributed an attempted attack on its own territory, against a supply line into Ukraine, and expelled diplomatic presence over it. Moved 5 to 6, still escalating.

Germany formally blamed Russia on 1 September for an attempted explosive drone attack on Leipzig/Halle airport in early August, near a Ukrainian cargo aircraft, and announced it will close Russia's consulate general in Bonn by 18 September, terminate the Russian House Berlin leases and tighten visa scrutiny. Russia denies it; Putin accuses Germany of planting evidence. US officials characterise the attempt as aimed at Ukraine's supply line inside NATO territory.

CYCyber / Tech8/10 · escalating ▲

An open-source agentic framework mapped 21 Taiwanese government systems in four days and reached a nuclear safety agency and seven-plus energy companies — the capability floor for a state-grade intrusion campaign just dropped.

Iran-attributed intrusions into US water systems continue; a multi-agent AI framework has now compromised a foreign government end-to-end with minimal human steering. | 29 Aug: no new joint advisory was found in the window; the CISA/FBI/EPA update expanding the PLC target set to Schneider Modicon M340 and Siemens S7-1200 is dated 23 July 2026 and predates this sweep. Held unchanged. | 6 Sept: no new joint advisory located in this window; the Iranian water-sector campaign reporting remains as recorded in August. Held.

ENEnergy / Markets8/10 · escalating ▲

Held at 8, moved from volatile to escalating: the week's move was consistently upward and war-driven, not two-way.

Brent closed the week of 4 September near $96, up about 9%, its strongest week since mid-July, on the resumed exchange and the strikes on Kuwait. The more consequential development is that the headline throughput number is itself now contested: US officials cite 10 to 18 million barrels a day while Lloyd's List Intelligence counts about 14 non-Iranian-linked ships a day and JMIC calls traffic far below baseline. Bessent separately forecast the strait would be 'worthless' within two years; analysts dispute that pipelines can substitute for it.

ALAlliance architecture5/10 · holding ▬

Architecture unchanged, but the pressure is now on the US guarantee rather than on the pact — the Washington Post reports Gulf states questioning the value of hosting American installations, which Washington rejects.

Two collective-defence pacts formed outside US auspices in 11 months; expansion of the newer one is now contested rather than imminent; NATO ramping to the Hague 5% standard. | 29 Aug: no change in defence obligations found. CNN reports Ratcliffe warned Russia against attacking NATO -- a US signal, not a change in who is obligated to defend whom, so it files to RU, not AL. Held unchanged. | 6 Sept: Iran struck US facilities in five host countries, which pressures the US guarantee but does not change who is obligated to defend whom — under this thread's own filing rule those are events in theatres and file to IR. No change in defence obligations found. Held.

Windward recorded the North Larak anchorage cluster rising to 35 tanker and cargo hulls on 12 August from 28 on 10 August, roughly 74 percent of them dark and ten of them sanctioned, and said Russia-to-Iran wet-cargo movements across the Caspian rose 2.9 times to 23 shipments in the 164 days after 28 February, with volumes going from 174,100 to about 437,000 barrels. "Iran isn't waiting for the blockade to lift. It's rerouting around it," Windward said. Kharg handles about 90 percent of Iran's oil exports.

03 — Detailed briefings

Actor & theatre briefings

13 briefings, synthesised and paraphrased from the source documents, each closing with a forward-looking assessment of likely near-term trajectory.

01 Homeland & Western Hemisphere+

The Homeland picture is dominated by narco-terrorism and border security. Mexico-based cartels — principally the Sinaloa Cartel and the New Generation Jalisco Cartel — remain the dominant suppliers of fentanyl, heroin, methamphetamine and South American cocaine to the U.S. market, while a wave of independent, semi-autonomous fentanyl producers has fragmented cartel control since 2020. Synthetic opioids killed more than 52,000 Americans in the 12 months to October 2024 — a 33% year-over-year drop that the ATA credits partly to wider naloxone access. China remains the top source of fentanyl precursor chemicals, with India second.

Enforcement has intensified sharply: Southwest border law-enforcement encounters fell 14% in 2024, and Border Patrol apprehensions dropped 85% year-over-year by January 2025. At the same time, cartel violence has escalated in Mexico itself — IED attacks on Mexican security forces surged from just 3 in 2020–2021 to nearly 1,600 in 2024, using landmines, mortars and grenades.

Policy has shifted decisively under the "Trump Corollary to the Monroe Doctrine": treating cartels as designated foreign terrorist organizations, running Operation SOUTHERN SPEAR against narco-terrorists across the hemisphere, and executing Operation ABSOLUTE RESOLVE against Nicolás Maduro's network in Venezuela. The NDS commits to guaranteeing U.S. military and commercial access to the Panama Canal, the Gulf of America, and Greenland, backed by a reshuffled Coast Guard/Navy posture and, where necessary, unilateral lethal action against cartels.

Homeland defense also spans Golden Dome missile and drone defense, nuclear-force modernization, cyber-defense build-out, and a "resource-sustainable" counterterrorism posture aimed only at Islamic terrorist actors with the intent and capability to strike the U.S. directly.

Forward outlook
  • Continued high-enforcement border posture and further cartel-fragmentation violence in Mexico.
  • Additional hemispheric access-assurance actions likely around Greenland, Panama and Venezuela.
  • Golden Dome and counter-UAS development continuing as flagship Homeland-defense programs through the rest of the decade.
ATA 2025NDS 2026NSS 2025
02 China (People's Republic of China)+

China is described across all three documents as the most comprehensive threat the U.S. faces — "the second most powerful country in the world" and, per the NDS, "the most powerful state relative to us since the 19th century." Xi Jinping's overarching goal is the "great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation" by 2049, with PLA modernization benchmarks set for 2027 and 2035 en route to a "world-class military."

Militarily, the PLA fields the DF-27 hypersonic-capable ballistic missile and the PCH191 long-range rocket launcher, and its third carrier, the Fujian, began sea trials in 2024 and is expected to reach full service around 2025–26. In cyberspace, the Volt Typhoon campaign has prepositioned access on U.S. critical infrastructure for use during a future crisis, while Salt Typhoon compromised U.S. telecommunications networks — together, the ATA calls this "the most active and persistent cyber threat" the U.S. faces.

Around Taiwan, Beijing has cut the island's formal diplomatic partners from 22 to 12 since 2016 and continues both economic coercion and military pressure, while confrontations with the Philippines in the South China Sea (2024) and with Japan near the Senkakus keep tensions elevated. China also weaponizes its dominance of critical minerals — banning gallium, germanium and antimony exports to the U.S. in December 2024 in retaliation for chip-export controls — and is racing toward AI leadership (a stated goal of displacing the U.S. as the top AI power by 2030), a $3.3 trillion bioeconomy, and lunar milestones (a 2024 sample-return mission, a crewed landing targeted for 2030, a lunar base targeted for 2035).

The NDS response is deliberately non-confrontational: "deter China in the Indo-Pacific through strength, not confrontation," expanding military-to-military communication with the PLA for stability and de-escalation while building a denial defense along the First Island Chain. The stated goal is not regime change or containment but a sustainable balance of power. The NSS frames this as economically existential too — the Indo-Pacific already generates roughly half of global GDP by purchasing-power parity, and Washington's ambition is to grow the U.S. economy from $30 trillion (2025) to $40 trillion in the 2030s alongside a rebalanced trade relationship with Beijing.

Forward outlook
  • Continued Taiwan pressure and diplomatic-isolation campaign through 2026.
  • Fujian reaching full operational service; PLA's 2027 modernization milestone as a key benchmark to watch.
  • Critical-minerals export restrictions likely to be reused as economic leverage in future frictions.
  • China projected to add more legacy-chip (28nm+) capacity than the rest of the world combined through 2028.
ATA 2025NDS 2026NSS 2025
03 Russia+

Russia views its war in Ukraine as a proxy conflict with the West, and as of the March 2025 ATA had "seized the upper hand," grinding toward continued territorial gains despite catastrophic losses — more than 750,000 dead and wounded since the February 2022 invasion, its worst toll since World War II. Russia's economy nonetheless remains the world's fourth largest by purchasing-power parity, sustained by trade with China, workarounds to sanctions, and continued defense-industrial investment.

Russia retains the world's largest and most diverse nuclear arsenal, a modernized and mobile strategic force, and an expanding non-strategic ("tactical") nuclear stockpile. Its chemical-weapons record includes two documented assassination attempts using Novichok nerve agent — against Sergei and Yulia Skripal in the U.K. (2018) and Aleksey Navalny (2020) — plus hundreds of alleged battlefield chemical-weapons uses against Ukrainian forces since late 2022. Moscow is also developing a satellite-based nuclear antisatellite weapon, first flagged after a February 2022 launch.

Cyber and influence capabilities round out the threat: deep experience integrating cyberattacks with wartime operations, and influence organizations like the Social Design Agency, ANO Dialog and RT working to erode confidence in U.S. elections and institutions. Domestically, Russia's chip industry lags badly (currently ~65nm, targeting 28nm by 2030), pushing deeper technical cooperation with China.

The NDS assesses Russia as a "persistent but manageable" threat to NATO's eastern flank rather than a challenger for European hegemony — non-U.S. NATO's $26 trillion economy dwarfs Russia's $2 trillion — and directs European allies, now committed to the 5%-of-GDP Hague standard, to take primary responsibility for conventional defense and Ukraine support, with the U.S. focused on Homeland defense and China.

Forward outlook
  • Continued attritional erosion of Ukraine's position absent a negotiated settlement, which both Moscow and Kyiv have shown some openness to.
  • Deepening Russia–China–Iran–North Korea linkages expected regardless of how the war ends.
  • NATO allies ramping toward the 5% GDP standard and assuming a larger share of Ukraine support through 2026 and beyond.
ATA 2025NDS 2026NSS 2025
04 Iran+

Iran's regional network — the so-called "Axis of Resistance" (Hizballah, Hamas, the Huthis, and Iraqi Shia militias) — has been severely degraded through 2024–25. Israeli strikes on Iranian air defenses in April and October 2024 preceded the collapse of Iran's Syrian ally Bashar al-Assad in December 2024, and by June 2025, Operation MIDNIGHT HAMMER saw U.S. forces strike and, per the NDS, "obliterate" Iran's nuclear program amid Israel's "12-Day War" with Iran. A separate U.S. campaign, Operation ROUGH RIDER, degraded Huthi strike capability enough to compel a ceasefire on Red Sea shipping attacks.

Even so, the ATA (published just before Midnight Hammer) assessed Khamenei had not reauthorized the nuclear-weapons program suspended in 2003, though internal pressure and eroding taboos around the subject were building. The NDS, writing after the strike, states Iran's leaders "have also left open the possibility that they will try again to obtain a nuclear weapon." Iran retains a large stockpile of missiles and UAVs, the region's largest, and continues to threaten shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. Tehran also maintains a long-running vendetta tied to the January 2020 killing of Qods Force commander Qasem Soleimani, and Iranian cyber actors (IRGC) breached a 2024 U.S. presidential campaign-linked email account for influence purposes.

Post-Assad Syria remains volatile: the HTS-led interim government has struggled to unify the country's ethnosectarian groups, and in early March 2025, HTS-aligned and jihadist forces killed more than 1,000 people — mostly Alawite and Christian civilians — in northwestern Syria. ISIS is actively working to exploit that instability to reconstitute.

Strategically, the U.S. now frames the Middle East as a region of opportunity rather than perpetual crisis: Israel as a "model ally" defending itself with limited backing, Gulf states increasingly capable of self-defense, and an expanding Abraham Accords framework.

Forward outlook
  • Close monitoring for renewed Iranian nuclear signaling or reconstitution efforts.
  • Proxy-network rebuilding attempts by Hizballah, Huthis and Iraqi militias, even in degraded form.
  • Syria's stabilization remains uncertain and is flagged as a potential ISIS-resurgence vector.
ATA 2025NDS 2026NSS 2025
05 North Korea (DPRK)+

Kim Jong Un's regime is increasingly bound to Moscow. The June 2024 Comprehensive Strategic Partnership treaty includes a mutual-defense clause Kim has cited to justify sending munitions, missiles and thousands of combat troops to fight for Russia in Ukraine — a relationship that also reduces Pyongyang's historic dependence on Beijing and gives North Korean forces rare modern combat experience.

In 2024, North Korea test-fired three intermediate-range ballistic missiles it claimed carried maneuverable hypersonic payloads, part of a steady buildup of its nuclear-warhead stockpile and missile-delivery sophistication. The ATA judges North Korea is "probably prepared to conduct a nuclear test" and continues ICBM flight testing capable of threatening the U.S. Homeland directly. Much of this is funded through large-scale cryptocurrency theft — hundreds of millions of dollars annually — alongside sanctioned trade in labor and UN-proscribed goods.

North Korea's conventional forces remain aging and Soviet-era, but its missile and WMD programs pose a growing, direct threat to South Korea, Japan, and increasingly the U.S. Homeland. Kim has historically relied on non-lethal coercive signaling (missile tests, balloon launches) but retains the option to escalate to lethal asymmetric action, including along the disputed Northern Limit Line.

The NDS assesses South Korea — with its strong economy, defense industry and conscription-based military — as capable of assuming primary responsibility for deterring North Korea, opening the door to a reduced U.S. force posture on the peninsula.

Forward outlook
  • Watch for a possible North Korean nuclear test.
  • Continued missile-testing cadence and deepening technical payoff from the Russia partnership.
  • Possible adjustments to U.S. force posture on the Korean Peninsula as Seoul assumes more responsibility.
ATA 2025NDS 2026
06 Transnational Crime & Terrorism+

Even in degraded form since the 2019 defeat of its physical caliphate, ISIS remains "the world's largest Islamic terrorist organization." Its branches vary sharply by capability and momentum: ISIS-Khorasan (South/Central Asia) is the most capable of external attacks and was linked to 2024 mass-casualty attacks in Russia and Iran; ISIS-Somalia doubled in size over the past year; ISIS-West Africa is the largest branch by claimed attacks; and ISIS-Sahel is expanding into coastal West Africa. The group's reach into the Homeland was demonstrated by the January 1, 2025 New Orleans attack and an October 2024 arrest of an Afghan national plotting an Election Day attack.

Al-Qa'ida's network remains active and diversified: AQAP relaunched its "Inspire" propaganda guide, al-Shabaab (its wealthiest affiliate) is deepening ties with the Huthis, and the group is expanding territorial influence in West Africa, including near U.S. personnel in Burkina Faso and Mali.

Financially motivated cybercrime is a parallel and growing threat: a mid-2024 ransomware attack on the largest U.S. healthcare payment processor disrupted prescriptions and even forced ambulance diversions, and both state-linked (2023) and purely criminal (October 2024) actors have struck U.S. water utilities. Transnational criminal organizations also launder billions through digital currencies and engage in human trafficking tied to migrant smuggling debt bondage.

Forward outlook
  • Africa-based ISIS branches (Somalia, West Africa, Sahel) likely to keep expanding.
  • Continued risk of ISIS-inspired, Homeland-directed "lone actor" attacks.
  • Ransomware and cyberattacks on U.S. critical infrastructure (healthcare, water) expected to persist.
ATA 2025NDS 2026
07 Europe & NATO+

The headline shift is burden-sharing: at the June 2025 NATO Hague Summit, allies committed to a new spending standard of 5% of GDP — 3.5% on core military spending plus 1.5% on broader security-related spending. Finland and Sweden's 2023–24 NATO accession extended the alliance's Arctic frontage, and the NDS explicitly wants European allies to take primary responsibility for their own conventional defense, including leading support for Ukraine, with the U.S. providing "critical but more limited" backing while it prioritizes Homeland defense and China.

The NSS frames Europe's challenges as running deeper than underspending, citing a decline in continental Europe's share of global GDP from 25% in 1990 to 14% today, alongside concerns about migration policy, demographic decline, and what it calls a loss of "civilizational self-confidence." Germany's continued reliance on Russian gas processed through Chinese facilities is cited as a cautionary example of the deeper economic entanglements the war has exposed.

On Ukraine specifically, U.S. policy is to press for an "expeditious cessation of hostilities" to stabilize European economies, prevent unintended escalation, and reestablish strategic stability with Moscow — while insisting that responsibility for both the war's resolution and Ukraine's reconstruction sits primarily with Europe.

Forward outlook
  • Continued diplomatic pressure toward a negotiated Ukraine settlement.
  • Allies ramping spending toward the 5% GDP standard through the remainder of the decade.
  • Gradual U.S. force-posture rebalancing away from Europe toward Homeland and Indo-Pacific priorities.
NDS 2026NSS 2025
08 Middle East+

The NSS frames the Middle East as receding from its decades-long position atop American foreign policy, thanks to U.S. energy independence and a run of 2025 diplomatic wins: an Israel–Iran de-escalation, an Egypt–Ethiopia agreement, a Gaza ceasefire with the return of all living hostages, and a Sharm el-Sheikh summit at which Arab states rallied behind a peace and normalization push. Gulf states, courted through Trump's May 2025 visits, are deepening AI-technology and defense partnerships with Washington.

Israel is described as a "model ally," defending itself with only limited U.S. support, and the U.S. aims to expand the Abraham Accords to more countries. Lebanon elected a president in January 2025 after a years-long vacancy, though further Hizballah–Israel conflict remains a live risk to that fragile progress. The Huthis, though degraded by Operation ROUGH RIDER, retain some capability, and Iraqi Shia militias continue pressuring the remaining U.S. presence in Iraq. The unresolved question of Gaza's post-conflict governance and West Bank instability are flagged as the region's most likely sources of renewed volatility.

Forward outlook
  • Further Abraham Accords expansion likely to be pursued.
  • Gaza reconstruction and governance remain unresolved — a flagged risk for renewed instability.
  • Persistent risk of a Hizballah–Israel flare-up in Lebanon.
ATA 2025NDS 2026NSS 2025
09 Africa+

Africa hosts some of the fastest-growing extremist franchises tracked in the ATA — ISIS-West Africa (the group's largest branch by claimed attacks), an expanding ISIS-Sahel, and al-Qa'ida gaining ground toward urban centers in Burkina Faso and Mali where U.S. personnel are stationed. The NSS calls for a deliberate pivot away from decades of aid-centered policy toward trade and investment, prioritizing critical minerals and energy development, and explicitly avoiding "long-term American presence or commitments."

The NDS narrows the U.S. military mission to preventing Islamic terrorists with the capability and intent to strike the Homeland from using African safe havens, while leaning on allies and partners to lead the fight against other regional terrorist groups. Diplomatically, the administration points to a 2025 DRC–Rwanda agreement as a model for resolving regional conflict, alongside stated interest in preventing an Ethiopia–Eritrea–Somalia conflict and addressing Sudan.

Forward outlook
  • Counterterrorism activity limited to direct-action strikes on Homeland-capable threats, not broader campaigns.
  • Investment- and minerals-led engagement likely to expand.
  • DRC–Rwanda peace implementation worth tracking as a template for future regional diplomacy.
ATA 2025NDS 2026NSS 2025
10 Technology, Space & Cyber+

This domain cuts across every actor. China's Volt Typhoon and Salt Typhoon campaigns represent the most persistent cyber threat to U.S. infrastructure and telecommunications; Beijing is also pursuing whole-of-government dominance in AI, biotechnology, quantum computing and semiconductors, with a documented history of large-scale intellectual-property theft (as much as 80% of U.S. economic-espionage cases circa 2021 involved PRC entities). Russia, constrained technologically by sanctions, is nonetheless deploying AI-generated deepfakes, AI-enabled counter-drone systems, and battlefield-tested electronic warfare, and is developing a nuclear antisatellite weapon. North Korea funds its weapons programs substantially through cryptocurrency theft, while Iran pairs offensive cyber operations with influence campaigns.

In space, China has "eclipsed Russia" as the second space power, operating the Beidou navigation constellation, ground-based counterspace weapons (jammers, directed-energy weapons, anti-satellite missiles), and an expanding low-Earth-orbit satellite-internet constellation, while pursuing crewed lunar milestones through 2030 and 2035.

On the U.S. side, the NDS's answer is Golden Dome for America — a next-generation missile and drone defense shield — paired with nuclear-force modernization, expanded cyber defenses, and the fourth line of effort: "Supercharge the U.S. Defense Industrial Base," reshoring production, adopting AI in manufacturing, and leveraging allied production capacity.

Forward outlook
  • 2026–2028 is a critical window in the legacy-chip capacity race and Golden Dome development.
  • Counterspace and antisatellite competition likely to intensify.
  • Continued cyber prepositioning on critical infrastructure by China and Russia should be expected.
ATA 2025NDS 2026
11 The Adversarial Cooperation Axis+

The ATA identifies deepening cooperation among China, Russia, Iran and North Korea as one of the most consequential trends in the threat picture — a set of primarily bilateral relationships that individually reinforce each actor's capabilities while collectively raising the risk that a conflict with any one adversary draws in another. Russia's war in Ukraine has been the accelerant: China provides dual-use materials and components that sustain Russia's defense-industrial base and has grown bilateral trade sharply since 2022; Iran supplies UAVs to Russia in exchange for technical support to its own weapons, intelligence and cyber programs; and North Korea has sent munitions, missiles and thousands of troops to fight for Russia under the June 2024 mutual-defense treaty.

China and Russia's relationship is judged to carry the greatest long-term risk to U.S. interests — more than a decade of combined military signaling has deepened into joint bomber patrols, naval operations, and a November 2024 agreement to expand cooperation on the Arctic's Northern Sea Route, an alternative to Western-dominated shipping lanes. The four also use forums like BRICS and the UN to pursue shared goals such as de-dollarization and to blunt U.S.-led pressure.

The ATA is careful to note this cooperation is uneven — driven mainly by a shared interest in circumventing U.S. power rather than genuine alignment, and tempered by each actor's own concerns about escalation and divergent interests.

Forward outlook
  • Axis cohesion is assessed likely to keep deepening through 2026, independent of the Ukraine war's outcome.
  • Arctic/Northern Sea Route cooperation and BRICS coordination are useful leading indicators to track.
ATA 2025
12 U.S. Strategic Posture — The Four Lines of Effort+

The 2026 National Defense Strategy organizes the Department of War's approach around four lines of effort:

1. Defend the U.S. Homeland — secure borders, guarantee access to key hemispheric terrain (Panama Canal, Gulf of America, Greenland), build Golden Dome missile/drone defense, modernize nuclear forces, harden cyber defenses, and maintain focused counterterrorism.

2. Deter China in the Indo-Pacific Through Strength, Not Confrontation — expand PLA military-to-military communication for stability, build a denial defense along the First Island Chain, and enable regional allies, aiming for a sustainable balance of power rather than domination.

3. Increase Burden-Sharing with U.S. Allies and Partners — press NATO toward the 5%-of-GDP Hague standard, push South Korea toward primary responsibility for deterring North Korea, empower Gulf and Israeli partners against Iran, and rely on regional partners to lead against lesser threats in Africa and the Western Hemisphere.

4. Supercharge the U.S. Defense Industrial Base — reshore defense production, expand non-traditional vendors, adopt AI in manufacturing, and leverage allied production capacity to arm both U.S. and partner forces at scale.

Named operations referenced throughout the documents: MIDNIGHT HAMMER (June 2025 strike on Iran's nuclear program), ABSOLUTE RESOLVE (action against Maduro's Venezuela-based network), SOUTHERN SPEAR (Western Hemisphere counter-narco-terrorism), and ROUGH RIDER (campaign that degraded Huthi strike capability and ended attacks on U.S. shipping).

NDS 2026
13 Net Assessment — Forward Outlook Through 2026 and Beyond+

Synthesizing the three documents' own stated goals, milestones and warnings — organized by horizon, from today (August 2026) outward. These are the documents' assessed trajectories, not guaranteed outcomes.

Near-term — rest of 2026
  • Continued NATO ally spending increases toward the 5%-of-GDP Hague standard.
  • Continued PRC pressure and diplomatic-isolation campaign against Taiwan; the Fujian carrier reaching full operational status.
  • Watch for North Korean nuclear-test signaling and continued ICBM/IRBM testing.
  • Ongoing monitoring of Iranian nuclear-reconstitution efforts and proxy-network rebuilding.
  • Russia–Ukraine likely to continue its attritional trajectory absent a negotiated settlement the U.S. is actively pushing.
  • Further hemispheric access-assurance actions around Greenland, Panama and Venezuela under the Trump Corollary.
  • Deepening China–Russia–Iran–North Korea cooperation across Arctic shipping, BRICS coordination, and defense-industrial linkages.
Mid-term — 2027 to 2030
  • 2027: PLA's first major counter-intervention modernization milestone.
  • 2028: China projected to out-build the rest of the world combined in legacy (28nm+) semiconductor capacity.
  • 2030: China's targeted deadline for global AI leadership and a crewed lunar landing.
  • 2030: Russia's targeted deadline for mass-producing domestic 28nm semiconductor chips.
  • 2030s: NSS-stated path from a $30 trillion (2025) to a $40 trillion U.S. economy.
Long-term — 2035 to 2049
  • 2035: PLA's second major modernization milestone; China's targeted deadline for a first lunar base.
  • 2049: Xi Jinping's "great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation" and "world-class military" target — the PRC's centenary.

Brief 0132026-09-06 · Sundaycutoff 2026-09-06T19:30Z

The war restarted. After about a month without a direct exchange the US struck Iran on 1 September, citing a failed Iranian attempt to mine the strait and hit a US base in Jordan, and Iran retaliated across five countries hosting US facilities — Kuwait, Bahrain, the UAE, Jordan and Iraq. The Qatari mediation channel that opened Brief 012's window is dead; Vance says there will be no talks until Iran stops attacking commercial shipping. Iran alleges a US strike killed civilians at a wedding in Sirik: the figures differ between outlets, Vance is 'extremely skeptical', CENTCOM says it does not target civilians, and the claim runs here unresolved. Separately, the one number everyone uses to judge whether Hormuz works is now itself in dispute — Treasury, Energy and the White House cite 10 to 18 million barrels a day while Lloyd's List Intelligence counts about 14 non-Iranian-linked ships a day and JMIC's 1 September advisory calls traffic far below baseline. Brent closed the week near $96, its strongest since mid-July. On Russia, the first reciprocal restraint of the war: Putin ordered a 72-hour pause on Kyiv, Zelenskyy reciprocated on Moscow, and Witkoff and Kushner met Putin for over three hours on 5 September and Zelenskyy on 6 September, with no breakthrough announced by any party. IR moves to 10 and escalating; EU to 6 after Germany formally blamed Russia for the Leipzig airport drone attack.

Brief 0122026-08-29 · Saturdaycutoff 2026-08-29T2200Z

A 114-hour catch-up covering 25-29 Aug. The window's largest development was diplomatic and was initially denied: CIA Director John Ratcliffe made an unannounced visit to Moscow on 25 Aug, Kremlin spokesman Peskov denied that day that any US-envoy talks were planned, and the Kremlin later confirmed the visit and said Putin had been briefed. Two days later Qatar's Prime Minister ran the first structured Hormuz mediation found since the Islamabad memorandum lapsed on 16 Aug -- a temporary corridor and possible joint mine-clearing -- while Iran's stated price stayed exactly where it was and Trump said he was 'not in a hurry'. Both channels opened alongside escalation, not instead of it: a tanker was struck in the strait (UKMTO 121-26) with JMIC holding Hormuz at SEVERE, Ukraine destroyed a second irreplaceable Tu-95MS at Engels-2 in six weeks, and Russia test-launched a mobile ICBM three days after Ratcliffe left. Brent fell more than 5% over the week the war's largest sanctions package took effect -- the market is pricing the mediation, not the sanctions. IR moves from escalating to volatile at 9. Two corrections run in this brief: the Haiti attack Brief 011 logged as roughly 30 dead on 24 Aug in fact killed at least 47 on 23 Aug at Kenscoff with more than 52 abducted, and Brief 011's own thread moves for KP and HL were never written into the live ledger, which had been serving pre-Brief-011 values for four days.

Schema notes
2026-08-09The Mecca Joint Defence Agreement does not fit the nine threads cleanly. Filed under Iran/Hormuz as a consequence of that war, but its subject is Gulf alliance architecture and the US security-guarantor role. If a second item of this kind appears, open a tenth thread (provisional code AL — Alliance architecture).
2026-08-09Tenth thread AL (Alliance architecture) opened at the two-item threshold. Direction vocabulary was built for threat threads; for AL it is redefined as rate of structural change and that redefinition is carried on the thread object itself.
2026-08-16The project copy of intel-ledger.json and the working-folder copy can silently diverge if a run updates one and cannot reach the other to complete Step 7 — confirmed the hard way on 16 Aug 2026 (see verification_log). Future runs: if you can only reach one copy, do not assume it is current. State the gap in verification_log[] and, for a cloud run with no device bridge, do not mint a new brief_number or archive[] entry from a ledger you cannot cross-check — a short situational note that does not touch brief_number is the safer product. A full reconciliation needs a session with access to both copies.
2026-09-06retired_claims[] added. BRIEFING-PROTOCOL.md Step 6 has always required validate.py to check that 'retired claims cannot reappear', swept across the dashboard, the archive and every daily-brief-*.html on disk. The check was never implemented because the schema had nowhere to record what counts as retired: sources[].status 'superseded' tracks a retired document, and nothing tracked a retired claim. Each entry carries id, claim, retired_on, retired_by_brief, reason, patterns[] (case-insensitive regexes matched against the visible text of rendered output) and exempt_files[]. A brief filed on or before retired_on is exempt automatically, because delivered briefs are never rewritten and necessarily still contain the claim they made; preserved RETRACTED-* files are exempt for the same reason. Adding a claim here is part of issuing a correction, not a separate housekeeping task.
2026-09-06The 23 inline free-text citations introduced from Brief 011 onward are backfilled into sources[] with real, recovered URLs, and timeline_additions_2026[].src now carries registry codes throughout. New sources[] entries use status 'cited' — a dated item a brief cited, as distinct from a standing document ('current') or a recurring tracker ('tracking') — so they do not inflate the current-primary-document count the dashboard displays. Each carries cited_as[], the original inline strings, so the pre-backfill form of every citation is preserved rather than erased. Note that the bare string 'Al Jazeera 27 Aug 2026' denoted two different articles in two different entries (the Qatar Hormuz talks and the Haiti Kenscoff attack); they are now AJ-HORMUZ-0827 and AJ-HAITI-0827. With no free-text citations left, validate.py treats an unregistered citation as a failure by default.

2026-08-16CONTINUITY — reconciliation of a second forked briefing run ("Brief 003")
A cloud-based scheduled task (created earlier today from an interactive session, without first confirming whether a desktop-bound schedule already existed for this project — the exact check Rule 0's point 2 requires) fired at 17:04:41Z against the project's copy of intel-ledger.json. That copy had been stale since approximately Brief 002 — nine threads, no archive[], no node_edges/node_topics/node_history, nine sources — because no prior run had synced a Step 7 write back through it after this working-folder ledger diverged ahead of it. The cloud session had no device bridge and could not detect that divergence; following its own instructions faithfully, it produced a genuine, individually well-verified brief from the only ledger it could see, numbered it 'Brief 003', and described the interval as a 173-hour, six-missed-run gap. Both the numbering and the gap narrative were artifacts of the stale copy, not of reality — this ledger was at Brief 006 with a 15 Aug 15:00Z cutoff at the time, one normal cycle behind. Separately and independently, a desktop-bound scheduled task with working-folder access produced this ledger's own Brief 007 within the same window, detected the fork by reading the project's copies directly, disclosed it in full on Brief 007's masthead, and correctly declined to renumber over it — but self-reported that its own project write access was refused, so Step 7 was left incomplete on that side too.		verified-primary
RECONCILED
